meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Your Liberty To Swing Your Fist Ends Just Where My Nose Begins'?
meta.ogDescription: Mill never wrote it. The earliest documented version comes from John B. Finch's temperance address in Iowa City, 7 May 1882.

answer.label: Not John Stuart Mill — earliest known: John B. Finch, 1882
answer.authorDates: 1852–1887 · American temperance orator, chairman of the Prohibition Party
answer.sourceLine: The sentence appears nowhere in On Liberty — the words nose and fist do not occur once in the full text — and no source has ever traced it to Mill. The earliest instance located by Quote Investigator ↗ is a temperance address John B. Finch gave at the Opera-House in Iowa City on 7 May 1882, printed in his collected speeches in 1887; his own wording was longer and clumsier than the one-liner that circulates today.

source.heading: The 1882 speech

docMeta.dd: The People Versus the Liquor Traffic: Speeches of John B. Finch
“The Defence Reviewed” — Opera-House, Iowa City, Sunday evening, 7 May 1882
Ed. Charles Arnold McCully (New York: The R.W.G. Lodge, 1887), pages 127–128
A later, much-shortened folk version — not Finch’s own wording

source.excerpt: This arm is my arm (and my wife’s), it is not yours. Up here I have a right to strike out with it as I please. I go over there with these gentlemen and swing my arm and exercise the natural right which you have granted; I hit one man on the nose, another under the ear, and as I go down the stairs on my head, I cry out: “Is not this a free country?” “Yes, sir.” “Have not I a right to swing my arm?” “Yes, but your right to swing your arm leaves off where my right not to have my nose struck begins.” Here civil government comes in to prevent bloodshed, adjust rights, and settle disputes.
trail: Mill’s text was searched, not assumed. The complete Project Gutenberg text of On Liberty ↗ (first published 1859) contains Mill’s actual harm principle — that the only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others — but not a single occurrence of the word “nose” or the word “fist”.

The earliest known instance was read in the original. The 1887 collection at the Internet Archive ↗ prints, at pages 127–128 of “The Defence Reviewed” (delivered at the Opera-House, Iowa City, 7 May 1882): “Yes, but your right to swing your arm leaves off where my right not to have my nose struck begins.”

The legal-canon version is Chafee’s, and he was quoting. Page 957 of “Freedom of Speech in War Time” ↗ (Harvard Law Review, June 1919) gives the words to a judge Chafee does not name: “Your right to swing your arms ends just where the other man’s nose begins.”

The specialist verdict. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes the saying began with Prohibitionist orators in a variety of formulations, that Finch communicated the earliest known instance in 1882, and that ascriptions to Lincoln and to Oliver Wendell Holmes have no support at this time.
source.excerptNote: Finch’s wording is longer and clumsier than the saying that circulates today. The compact “fist … nose” one-liner is the product of decades of retelling by other speakers, not a sentence anyone is documented as having written in that form first.

artifact.linkText: Read the speech at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: The passage quoted above comes from The People Versus the Liquor Traffic, published in 1887 — far earlier than the 1931 line for US copyright — so Finch’s text is in the public domain, as is the scan of it at the Internet Archive ↗. The shortened modern one-liner has no identifiable author or first publication of its own; it circulates as a folk saying rather than as anyone’s copyrighted sentence.

author.name: John B. Finch
author.heading: Who was John B. Finch?
author.metaLine: 1852–1887 · American temperance orator & chairman of the Prohibition Party
author.bio: John Bird Finch (17 March 1852 – 3 October 1887) was an American educator turned professional temperance orator who rose to chair the Prohibition Party in the mid-1880s. He toured the United States and Canada arguing the case for prohibition as a mock courtroom trial — The People Versus the Liquor Traffic — and the fist-and-nose illustration was one of his set pieces, a bit of physical comedy used to show that personal liberty has edges. He died in Boston in 1887, the same year his speeches were collected into the volume that preserves the earliest known version of the saying.

misattribution.heading: Three false credits, one popularizer
misattribution.intro: This saying is a quotation magnet: the same idea circulates in at least three wordings, each pinned to a different luminary. Quote Investigator ↗ checked all of them.

items.scope: Usually the “swing my arms in any direction” wording
items.why: QI found no evidence Mill ever used the phrase. The link seems to run through Richard Posner, who in 1992 boiled the philosophy of On Liberty down to “Your rights end where his nose begins” — a summary of Mill’s position, and, as QI notes, without any claim that Mill said it. An independent word-search of the full Project Gutenberg text of On Liberty ↗ returns no instance of “nose” or “fist” at all.

items.scope: The “right to swing my fist” wording
items.why: The most common modern credit, and QI ↗ has found nothing to support it. The earliest ascriptions it documents are hedged or late: a 1970 humour column credited “Oliver Wendell Holmes or someone like him”, and a 1989 city councilor quoted a Holmes version while defending a smoking ban.

items.scope: The “my right to swing my fist” wording
items.why: QI ↗ found no support for the connection. Its example is a 1980 letter to the Dallas Morning News invoking “the old Abraham Lincoln concept” — more than nine decades after the saying was already in print.

items.scope: The “your right to swing your arms” wording
items.why: Chafee really did print it, in the Harvard Law Review for June 1919 — but he attributed it to a judge he did not name, in a hypothetical about a man arrested for swinging his arms. You can read the sentence at page 957 of the scanned article ↗. He carried the saying into law; he did not coin it.

misattribution.truthLine: The saying appears to have grown up among prohibitionist orators in the 1880s, and QI ↗ concludes that John B. Finch delivered the earliest known instance, in 1882.

context.heading: A free-speech slogan that started as a prohibition argument
lead: Today the line is standard-issue civil libertarianism, reached for in arguments about free speech, smoking bans, mask rules and gun laws. Its documented origin points almost the other way. The early versions traced by Quote Investigator ↗ come overwhelmingly off the American temperance platform, where prohibitionists used it to argue that a man’s personal liberty to drink stopped at the harm his drinking did to everyone around him.

Finch’s own version is stage business rather than epigram: he swings his arm, hits one man on the nose and another under the ear, and goes down the stairs on his head still shouting about a free country. The line got shorter every time it was retold. By 1894 a temperance campaigner, Rev. A. C. Dixon, was using “your liberty ends just where my nose begins”; by 1902 the chancellor of the University of Georgia was recommending “my right to swing my arm ends where your nose begins” to teachers as the way to fix the principle in a child’s mind.
context.detailsSummary: How it got into law books
detailsBody: The saying entered legal discourse in June 1919, when Zechariah Chafee Jr. used it in “Freedom of Speech in War Time” in the Harvard Law Review. Chafee did not claim it: he put it in the mouth of an unnamed judge sentencing a man arrested for swinging his arms. The article was influential enough that a US senator had it reprinted as a Senate document, which is a large part of why the line now reads as a legal maxim rather than a revival-tent joke.

The Mill connection appears to be retrofitted. In 1992 the legal theorist Richard Posner summed up the philosophy of Mill’s On Liberty in seven words — “Your rights end where his nose begins” — as a gloss on Mill’s idea, not as a quotation from him. Mill’s actual formulation of the harm principle is drier and much longer.
context.pull: A slogan now used to defend liberty was invented to argue for prohibition.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI's earliest located instance of the saying is John B. Finch's 1882 Iowa City address; QI found no evidence Mill ever used the phrase (citing only Posner's 1992 gloss on On Liberty, which did not claim Mill said it), no evidence for Oliver Wendell Holmes, and no support for Abraham Lincoln; Chafee's 1919 Harvard Law Review article credited the words to an anonymous judge; QI also documents the 1894 Dixon wording, the 1902 Walter B. Hill wording, the 1970 Bill Vaughan column and the 1980 Dallas Morning News letter.

The 1887 collection 'The People Versus the Liquor Traffic. Speeches of John B. Finch' (ed. Charles Arnold McCully, New York: The R.W.G. Lodge, 1887) contains Speech VI, 'The Defence Reviewed', headed 'An Address delivered at the Opera-House, Iowa City, Sunday evening, May 7, 1882', and prints at pages 127-128: 'Yes, but your right to swing your arm leaves off where my right not to have my nose struck begins.'

The full Project Gutenberg text of John Stuart Mill's On Liberty contains the harm-principle sentence ('That the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others.') and contains zero occurrences of the word 'nose' and zero occurrences of the word 'fist'.
Project Gutenberg ebook 34901 is On Liberty by John Stuart Mill, described there as an essay published in 1859, with the complete text freely available.

Zechariah Chafee Jr., 'Freedom of Speech in War Time' (Harvard Law Review, 1919), at page 957, describes a man arrested for swinging his arms and hitting another in the nose and quotes: 'Your right to swing your arms ends just where the other man's nose begins.'
John Bird Finch (March 17, 1852 - October 3, 1887) was an American politician and educator who served as chairman of the Prohibition Party; born in Lincklaen, New York, died in Boston, Massachusetts.
Wikiquote's John Stuart Mill page contains no entry for the fist/arm/nose saying in any section (neither sourced, disputed, nor misattributed).
John Stuart Mill's On Liberty was first published in 1859.
